name: Background job queue
needs: the AI step takes 40 seconds and the page hangs
generate a PDF without making the user wait
process an upload after it finishes
call a slow API without blocking the page
summary: The web request saves a job and answers right away. A separate worker picks up the job, does the slow part and stores the result. The page checks back for it.
need_when: A step takes more than a few seconds: LLM calls, video or image work, PDFs, big exports.
A step calls an outside service that can fail and should be retried.
skip_when: The work is fast and you need the answer before you can reply to the user.

ways.title: A jobs table in the database you already have
ways.how: Workers claim rows with a lock (Postgres FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED). Libraries: pg-boss (Node), River (Go), good_job (Rails), or a small model in Django.
ways.tradeoff: No new service to run. Fine for modest volume. Polling adds a little database load.

ways.title: A Redis-backed queue
ways.how: Celery or RQ for Python, BullMQ for Node.
ways.tradeoff: Fast and common, but it is one more service to run and monitor, and Redis persistence settings decide whether queued jobs survive a restart.

ways.title: A hosted background job service
ways.how: Inngest or Trigger.dev run steps for you and call back into your code.
ways.tradeoff: Less to operate. Another account, your data leaves your server, and moving off it later is work.

prompt:
Move [slow task] out of the web request into a background job.

Requirements:
- On request: validate input, create a job row (status pending, dedupe key, owner), and return 202 with the job id within 500 ms.
- A worker claims jobs with a lease (token plus claimed_at). If a worker dies, the job becomes claimable again after the lease expires.
- Retry with backoff up to [3] attempts, then mark it failed with a short error code. No stack traces or user data in that field.
- Add a status endpoint that returns pending, running, done or failed, plus the result link when done. Only the owner can read it.
- Cap active jobs per user and in total. Return 429 or 503 with a plain message when full.
- The page polls the status endpoint every [2] seconds and shows progress.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. The request returns in under 500 ms even when the task takes 60 seconds.
2. Killing the worker in the middle of a job and restarting it finishes the job exactly once.
3. Submitting the same request twice quickly creates one job.
4. A task that always fails ends as failed after the max attempts and the page says so.
5. Changing the job id in the URL can't show another user's job.
acceptance_checks: The request returns in under 500 ms even when the task takes 60 seconds.
Killing the worker in the middle of a job and restarting it finishes the job exactly once.
Submitting the same request twice quickly creates one job.
A task that always fails ends as failed after the max attempts and the page says so.
Changing the job id in the URL can't show another user's job.
if_you_skip_it: Requests time out behind your proxy, users click again and start duplicate work, and one slow call ties up the whole server.
how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal runs exports as queued jobs stored in Postgres. Each job has a dedupe key, a lease token and a max attempt count. Jobs with expired leases go back into the queue, or fail after the last attempt. There are caps on active exports per user and in total: a user with an export already running gets a 429, and a full queue returns 503.
